summary: This informational RFC gives guidelines for implementing the optional application-layer FEC protocol in the DVB-IPTV specification. It protects streaming media with two layers: a base layer using 1-D interleaved parity, and an enhancement layer based on the Raptor code.

eli5.summary: TV streams carry backup information in two layers, a simple one and a stronger one, so lost bits can be recovered.

how does dvb-iptv protect against packet loss

subtitle: Two-layer error protection for streaming video over IP networks

tldr.problem: Streaming video over IP networks can lose packets due to network impairments, degrading the viewer's experience. Simple protection schemes are either weak or expensive.
tldr.mechanism: DVB-IPTV applies two layers of forward error correction: a base layer using interleaved parity codes to handle bursty losses, and an optional enhancement layer using Raptor fountain codes for additional recovery.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can recover lost packets at the cost of sending repair data alongside the main stream. The enhancement layer is optional, so implementations can choose the trade-off that fits their constraints.

today: RFC 6683 is an Informational document providing implementation guidance for DVB-IPTV FEC. It has not been obsoleted, so it remains current as the authoritative guide for implementing this two-layer FEC protocol.

sections.title: Why DVB-IPTV Needs FEC Protection
sections.content:
Television broadcasters sending MPEG-2 streams over IP networks face packet loss from congestion, bit errors, and link failures. Without protection, viewers see freezes or artifacts. Forward Error Correction (FEC) adds redundant data that allows receivers to reconstruct lost packets, similar to how QR codes remain readable with damage.

The Digital Video Broadcasting - IPTV standard defines an optional application-layer FEC protocol in its technical specification. This RFC explains how to implement it using two published FEC standards: the 1-D interleaved parity code and the Raptor code.
sections.eli5: TV broadcasters send your favorite show over the internet, but some packets might get lost. FEC is like sending backup copies so the receiver can fix broken packets without asking for a resend.

sections.title: The Two-Layer Protection Approach
sections.content:
DVB-IPTV AL-FEC uses a systematic approach: the original media packets are sent unchanged, plus separate repair packets are sent in parallel streams. The receiver only uses repair packets if packets are lost.

The base layer uses 1-D interleaved parity, a simple method where a group of D by L source packets are XORed (exclusive OR) in a specific pattern to generate L repair packets. This pattern is effective at recovering bursts of lost packets up to length L. The method is similar to RAID disk arrays: if you know some values and the XOR result, you can compute the missing values.

The enhancement layer uses the Raptor code, a fountain code that can generate unlimited repair symbols on demand. A receiver only needs to collect any K + N symbols (where K is the original count) to recover all K original packets. Raptor scales well to large losses and variable network conditions.

A receiver supporting only the base layer can still recover many lost packets. A receiver supporting both layers gains higher recovery, especially against random loss patterns.
sections.eli5: The base layer is like a safety net with holes: it catches some falls. The enhancement layer is like a second, finer net underneath—if you fall through the first one, the second catches you. You can use just the first net if that's all you can handle.

sections.title: How Decoders Recover Lost Packets
sections.content:
A receiver using only the base-layer decoder processes parity repair packets to recover any missing source packets, then outputs the result. If the loss is heavier than the base layer can handle, some packets remain lost.

A receiver supporting hybrid (enhanced) decoding follows three steps. First, it runs the parity decoder to recover as many missing packets as possible. Second, if packets are still missing, it runs the Raptor decoder using both the received source packets and the packets recovered in step one. Third, if the Raptor decoder still leaves gaps, it converts unprocessed parity repair packets into a form the Raptor decoder can use, then runs Raptor again with this additional information.

This layered approach allows the protocol to gracefully adapt: loss recovery improves as more layers are enabled, but a basic implementation is still useful.
sections.eli5: Try the simple repair first. If it doesn't fix everything, try the advanced repair. If that still leaves holes, use both repairs together for a final attempt.

sections.title: Signaling and Compatibility Notes
sections.content:
The sender announces the FEC parameters out-of-band using the Session Description Protocol (SDP), which describes the multicast groups and ports for source and repair streams. An SDP example groups the source stream (mid:S1), a base-layer FEC stream (mid:R1), and an enhancement-layer FEC stream (mid:R2) using FEC grouping semantics.

Implementation requires careful attention to RTP header fields. The original DVB-IPTV specification required some non-standard RTP behavior—for example, setting the Synchronization Source (SSRC) field of FEC packets to zero, which violates RFC 3550. The RFC 6015 payload format addresses these issues but is not backward compatible with some deployed DVB equipment. This document lists the exceptions implementers must handle to stay compatible with the DVB-IPTV specification while building on RFC 6015.
sections.eli5: The sender says 'I'll send the main video here, backup copies here, and super-backups there' using a standard description. But some DVB devices broke the RTP rules, so new implementations must handle both the new correct way and the old non-standard way.

fields.name: Source Stream
fields.desc: Original MPEG-2 TS packets, sent unchanged.
